detection_signature: Image ends with powershell.exe AND CommandLine contains -EncodedCommand or -enc with a base64 payload >100 chars
explanation: T1059.001 covers adversaries running PowerShell. Encoded commands are a strong signal because they hide the actual payload from straightforward log review; legitimate admin scripts occasionally use -EncodedCommand to avoid quoting issues but the long base64 payload combined with bypass policy is suspicious. Analyst next step: base64-decode the EncodedCommand and inspect the actual script.
false_positive_examples: Legitimate admin remote scripts that use -EncodedCommand for quote safety

technique_name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell
detection_signature: cmd.exe spawning an obfuscated downloader chain; ParentImage in user temp directory
explanation: T1059.003 is cmd.exe execution. The chained download-and-iex pattern is the canonical drive-by stage-1 delivery. ParentImage in %TEMP% means the user just ran a downloaded executable; this is post-initial-access activity.
false_positive_examples: Software installers that legitimately download additional components

detection_signature: Process access where TargetImage is lsass.exe AND GrantedAccess is 0x1010, 0x1410, 0x1438, or 0x143A
explanation: T1003.001 is LSASS memory dumping. The GrantedAccess values 0x1010/0x1410/0x1438/0x143A correspond to PROCESS_VM_READ + PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION combinations needed to read LSASS memory pages. mimikatz, procdump, comsvcs.dll!MiniDump, and most credential dumpers leave this signature. EDR products tend to flag this immediately.
false_positive_examples: Some endpoint protection tools legitimately read LSASS for memory scanning

detection_signature: Successful logon (4624) with LogonType 10 (RemoteInteractive/RDP) from a public IP for an account that hasn't authenticated from that geography in the past 90 days
explanation: T1078 (Valid Accounts) is the use of stolen credentials. The signal here is the *combination*: LogonType 10 means RDP, the IpAddress is non-RFC1918 (public), and ideally the SIEM has enriched with 'first time this account has logged on from this IP/geo'. Without the enrichment, public-IP RDP logons are still notable enough to alert on.
false_positive_examples: Authorized remote work over RDP with VPN that NATs to a public IP

technique_name: Boot or Logon Autostart: Registry Run Keys
detection_signature: Registry SetValue under \CurrentVersion\Run or \RunOnce where Details points at an executable in %TEMP%, %APPDATA%, %ProgramData%, or another user-writable path
explanation: T1547.001 is autostart via Run keys. Legitimate software installs persistence under \Run too, but it points at Program Files or vendor-specific paths under HKLM. User-temp paths are nearly always malicious. The Image field tells you which process wrote the value; if it's also in user temp, that's a dropper installing persistence.
false_positive_examples: Some user-mode software (cloud sync clients, IM apps) install Run keys pointing into AppData\Local

technique_name: Create or Modify System Process: Windows Service
detection_signature: New service installation (7045) where ImagePath points outside System32 / Program Files AND service runs as LocalSystem with auto start
explanation: T1543.003 is service-based persistence. Legit software installers create services but their ImagePaths are under Program Files. ImagePath in C:\Users\Public, %TEMP%, or %APPDATA%, combined with LocalSystem and auto-start, is malicious nearly 100% of the time. The 7045 event is the canonical signal.
false_positive_examples: A few legitimate cross-vendor services (e.g. some VPN clients) install in user-writable paths

detection_signature: Rapid-fire FileCreate (11) events where TargetFilename matches the regex .*\.(locked|encrypted|crypted|enc|crypt|cry|kraken|wnry|wcry)$ across many directories
explanation: T1486 is ransomware encryption. The signature is the volume + extension pattern: hundreds of files getting renamed to a custom extension within minutes, all from the same Image. By the time you see this in real time it's mostly too late; the value is in alerting fast enough to stop further hosts from being hit and isolating the source process.
false_positive_examples: Some legitimate backup software produces .enc / .crypt files but at much lower volume

detection_signature: Object delete (4660) on backup-pattern paths (\Backups\, .bak, .vhd, snapshot files) by an interactive process (cmd / powershell / explorer)
explanation: T1485 is destruction of backups, typically a precursor to ransomware. The deletion of .bak / .vhd / VSS snapshots removes recovery options before encryption hits. Detection requires audit-on-delete configured for backup directories; without that, the events don't fire.
false_positive_examples: Backup retention scripts that legitimately delete old backups, but those usually run as service accounts not interactive

detection_signature: where.exe / dir / tree spawned with patterns matching credential-storing files (password, *.kdbx, id_rsa, *.ovpn, secret)
explanation: T1083 is file/directory enumeration, post-initial-access. The signal here is *what* is being searched for: filename patterns commonly tied to credentials (KeePass kdbx, SSH private keys, OpenVPN configs, files containing 'password'). Generic dir/where calls without these patterns are too noisy; the keyword filter is the value.
false_positive_examples: Sysadmins occasionally search for password files for legitimate password-rotation cleanup

detection_signature: net.exe view, nltest /domain_trusts, dsquery, or PowerShell Get-ADComputer / Get-ADUser used by a non-admin account or in rapid succession
explanation: T1018 is mapping the AD topology after initial access. nltest /domain_trusts and net view are the canonical commands attackers run to identify lateral-movement targets. Legitimate AD admin work generates similar logs but during business hours from admin accounts; the indicator is *who* and *when*.
false_positive_examples: AD administrators legitimately run these commands during routine domain audits

detection_signature: Successful 4624 with LogonType 10 from an internal IP that's not the user's normal workstation, especially during off-hours
explanation: T1021.001 is lateral movement via RDP. Distinct from T1078 (which assumes external entry); here the source IP is internal RFC1918 but unusual for the target user. Detection needs SIEM enrichment of the user's typical source-host pattern, otherwise legitimate help-desk RDP gets flagged.
false_positive_examples: IT support tickets that involve admin RDPing to a user workstation to troubleshoot

detection_signature: Network share access (5140) on ADMIN$ or C$ from a user account that's not in the Domain Admins group
explanation: T1021.002 is lateral movement via the hidden admin shares. ADMIN$/C$ access requires admin rights on the target; if the SubjectUserName is a regular user, either credentials were stolen (T1003) or admin shares are misconfigured. Either way, alert.
false_positive_examples: Patch management tools that authenticate with delegated admin rights

detection_signature: Bursts of 4625 (failed logon) for the same TargetUserName from one IP, OR for many TargetUserNames from one IP (password spray)
explanation: T1110 covers brute force and password spray. The Status 0xC000006D + SubStatus 0xC000006A is 'wrong password.' Bursts on a single account = brute force; spray across many accounts = password spray. Both deserve immediate alerts and source-IP block.
false_positive_examples: Forgotten password retry by a legitimate user, but normally <5 attempts

technique_name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Unix Shell
detection_signature: bash / sh executed with a piped curl|bash or wget|sh pattern, especially from a parent like sshd or web-server processes
explanation: T1059.004 is Unix shell execution. The curl-piped-to-bash pattern is the canonical Linux drive-by. Parent of sshd means SSH-delivered post-exploitation; parent of nginx/apache means webshell-driven RCE.
false_positive_examples: Some legitimate install scripts (Homebrew, Docker, etc.) use curl|sh as their first-time install pattern

detection_signature: Outbound HTTPS POSTs to a domain that resolves to an IP not seen in the prior 30 days, at regular jittered intervals (every 60-300s), with consistent payload size pattern
explanation: T1071.001 is C2 over web protocols. The signal isn't a single request, it's the *pattern*: regular intervals (beacon-style), unusual destination, consistent payload size. Modern C2 frameworks (Cobalt Strike, Sliver, Mythic) all do this. Detection requires the SIEM to compute beacon-like statistics over a time window.
false_positive_examples: Cloud SDK heartbeats, software auto-updaters, telemetry agents

detection_signature: File creation under /var/www, /inetpub, /wwwroot of a .php / .jsp / .asp / .aspx file by the web-server process AND in a directory not normally containing executable scripts (uploads, images, static)
explanation: T1505.003 is webshell drop. Web servers should only execute scripts from a controlled set of paths. A new .php in /uploads/ owned by www-data means an attacker uploaded the file via a vulnerable upload endpoint. This is post-exploitation; the next move will be HTTP requests to the webshell from external IPs.
false_positive_examples: Legitimate CMS plugin updates can write to web-root paths but usually under specific plugin directories

sample_log_line: 1683724850 198.51.100.42 - - [15/Apr/2026:11:42:00 +0000] "GET /api/v1/users?id=1' UNION SELECT username,password FROM users-- HTTP/1.1" 200 1842 "-" "sqlmap/1.7.2"
detection_signature: URI containing SQLi/XSS/path-traversal/RCE patterns (' UNION SELECT, <script>, ../../etc, ${jndi:ldap://, etc.) AND non-4xx response code
explanation: T1190 is exploitation of a public-facing app. The sqlmap user-agent is a giveaway; real attackers spoof. The signal is the URI patterns: SQL union, JNDI lookups, path traversal, command injection. Non-4xx response means the exploit didn't error out - either it succeeded or the server returned blind.
false_positive_examples: Penetration testing windows where the team is exercising the same patterns intentionally

detection_signature: Inbound email with macro-enabled attachment (.docm/.xlsm/.dotm/.xltm) AND sender domain not in the org's vendor allowlist
explanation: T1566.001 is spearphishing with attachment. The macro-enabled file extension is the marker; legitimate vendors send PDF or non-macro Office files. Modern email gateways block .docm/.xlsm by default unless from a trusted sender; the alert is when one slips through.
false_positive_examples: Internal automation that legitimately uses .xlsm for templates with vetted macros

detection_signature: CommandLine matches a base64 regex of length >= 200 chars AND Image is one of powershell.exe / cmd.exe / cscript.exe / wscript.exe / mshta.exe
explanation: T1027 is obfuscation. Long base64 in command lines is the canonical small-LM-detectable signal. Legitimate uses (jq scripts, encoded XML config) exist but are rare in cmd-shell context. The high-entropy + length combination is the discriminator.
false_positive_examples: Some build automation passes encoded JSON config via command line

detection_signature: rundll32.exe spawned with javascript: protocol or 'mshtml,RunHTMLApplication' patterns in the command line
explanation: T1218.011 is rundll32 abuse for proxy execution, bypassing application allowlists that trust rundll32 itself. The javascript: URI scheme through rundll32 + mshtml is the canonical pattern. Legitimate uses are essentially zero; flag with high confidence.
false_positive_examples: (none) - this is one of the cleanest detections; legitimate rundll32 invocations always reference DLL paths, not javascript:

detection_signature: certutil.exe with -decode, -decodehex, or -urlcache flags
explanation: T1140 is decoding staged payloads. certutil is a Windows-signed binary that includes base64/hex decoding as a side feature; attackers chain it as a download-and-decode primitive that lives off the land. PKI admins legitimately use certutil but rarely with -decode against arbitrary files.
false_positive_examples: PKI administrators who legitimately decode certificate blobs

detection_signature: Image is a signed Microsoft / well-known-vendor binary AND ImageLoaded is in the same directory AND ImageLoaded is unsigned OR has no OriginalFileName
explanation: T1574.002 is DLL side-loading. Attackers drop a malicious DLL alongside a signed legitimate executable that searches the local directory before System32. The signed app loads the malicious DLL with the app's trust. Detection: signed-Image + unsigned-ImageLoaded + same-directory.
false_positive_examples: Some legitimate vendors ship unsigned helper DLLs alongside their signed mains

sample_log_line: <Event><EventID>1</EventID><Image>C:\Users\victim\AppData\Local\Temp\loader.exe</Image><CommandLine>loader.exe</CommandLine></Event><FollowOnEvents><EventID>1</EventID><Image>C:\Windows\System32\wmic.exe</Image><CommandLine>wmic computersystem get model,manufacturer / wmic bios get serialnumber</CommandLine>
detection_signature: wmic queries against computersystem / bios / cpu fields shortly after a process launch from user-temp paths
explanation: T1497 is sandbox evasion. The loader does WMI queries to detect VirtualBox/VMware/Hyper-V via manufacturer strings and BIOS fingerprints; if a sandbox is detected, malware skips activation. Pattern: temp-loader spawns wmic with these specific queries within seconds.
false_positive_examples: Inventory scripts legitimately query computersystem for asset management

detection_signature: Registry SetValue under \SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows Defender\ disabling realtime / behaviour / cloud / IOAV protections
explanation: T1112 covers registry-based defense evasion. Disabling Defender via the registry is one of the highest-confidence T1112 indicators. Legitimate use of these keys is via Group Policy from a Domain Controller; direct registry manipulation by a non-GPO process is malicious.
false_positive_examples: Group Policy enforcement during initial domain join sets these values legitimately

detection_signature: Process not in the Chrome / Edge / Firefox vendor path reading or copying \AppData\Local\<browser>\User Data\Default\Login Data
explanation: T1555 covers credential theft from password stores. Browser Login Data files are SQLite databases of saved passwords. The decryption key (Local State -> os_crypt -> encrypted_key) needs to be stolen too. Pattern: a non-browser process accessing both files within seconds.
false_positive_examples: Some password manager import tools legitimately read these files (with user consent)

detection_signature: User account creation (4720) by a SubjectUserName that is not in the IT helpdesk / domain admin group
explanation: T1136 is creating new accounts for persistence. Legitimate account creation flows through IT/HR; an account creation by a non-admin user is suspicious. Pair with 4728 (added to Domain Admins) to catch the privilege-escalation chain.
false_positive_examples: Delegated account creation rights given to specific business units (HR, finance) for contractor onboarding

detection_signature: Add to security-enabled global group (4728) where MemberSid resolves to Domain Admins (RID 512), Enterprise Admins (RID 519), or Schema Admins (RID 518)
explanation: T1098 is account manipulation - typically privilege escalation by adding a compromised account to high-privilege AD groups. The 4728 + RID 512/519/518 combination is one of the most critical AD events to alert on at all times.
false_positive_examples: Legitimate IT promotions / role changes, but should always go through change management

technique_name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Visual Basic
detection_signature: wscript.exe / cscript.exe spawned by an Office process (winword/excel/powerpnt) executing a .vbs / .vbe / .js file from user-temp/downloads
explanation: T1059.005 covers VBS/JScript execution. The signal is the parent-child relationship: Office spawning wscript means a macro just executed an external script. Legitimate Office workflows nearly never produce this chain; it's almost always macro-based malware delivery.
false_positive_examples: Some enterprise Office templates with vetted macros do legitimately call wscript

detection_signature: DNS queries to a single domain with subdomains containing >50-char base64-like strings, at high frequency (>20/min)
explanation: DNS tunneling for exfiltration. Each TXT or A query encodes a chunk of data in the subdomain label; the resolver aggregation gives the attacker the data. Detection: per-domain entropy + query length distribution is the cleanest signal, since legitimate DNS rarely has long random-looking subdomains.
false_positive_examples: Some CDN cache-busting and DNS-based content delivery use long subdomain labels but with predictable patterns

detection_signature: Auto-elevating Windows binaries (fodhelper.exe, computerdefaults.exe, sdclt.exe) launching High integrity from a Medium-integrity parent in user-writable paths
explanation: T1548.002 is UAC bypass. The fodhelper / computerdefaults / sdclt binaries auto-elevate without UAC prompt by design, and abuse the registry to redirect execution. Pattern: auto-elevator with parent in user-temp/appdata = bypass attempt.
false_positive_examples: (rare) some legitimate installers exploit the same auto-elevation paths
